content.text:
I'm testing whether diagonal parity from the point determines cell colors, checking example 3 where the point is at (5,7) and comparing coordinate sums to see which values fill the even-parity cells.

Mapping out the actual 7-colored positions row by row, I notice they trace two diagonals crossing through the point (5,7): one running up-left to down-right, another up-right to down-left. These diagonals seem to bounce off the grid edges rather than continuing straight, since the pattern breaks near the bottom rows where 3s appear instead of expected 7s.

The 3-marked cells form their own smaller diamond pattern separate from the 7-diagonals, appearing symmetrically at rows 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 with consistent column offsets—likely a secondary reflection or a distinct shape overlaid on the main diagonal cross.

Looking at the second example with 5 placed at (1,2) in a 9x9 grid, I trace out the resulting diamond arrangement: 3s and 1s form clusters that seem to radiate from certain center points, with 1s at hollow centers and either 3s or the original 5 marking the diamond edges depending on distance from the seed point.

Remaining spots are 5s. Now examining example 1 with the 9 marker at (5,3) on a 10x10 grid, tracing where 3s, 9s, and 1s land row by row to find the underlying pattern.

I notice diamond-shaped units emerge — a 1 at the center surrounded by 3s at the four diagonal corners. I'm checking each candidate center against its corners to confirm the diamond structure, verifying that (1,3), (5,5), (5,7), and (7,3) all form valid diamonds with 3s at their corners. Now I'm trying to figure out where these diamond centers are positioned relative to the original 9 marker.

I'm second-guessing the offset pattern since some corner cells partially appear but others don't quite fit, so I'm considering whether the diamonds actually come from diagonal rays bouncing off the grid walls from the source point instead.

I'm tracing that reflection path step by step but the directions keep flipping in ways that don't cleanly match the 9s in the grid, so I'm listing out all the coordinates marked 9 in the first example to check against a traced ray going down-left from the source.

Continuing the trace, the path closes back on itself into a loop after bouncing off the bottom edge—confirming it's a closed billiard trajectory. Now I'm checking which cells get marked 3 or 1 instead of 9, wondering if those are crossing points where multiple paths intersect.

Tracing the r+c=8 diagonal line across the grid, I notice it hits value 3 at (4,4) and (6,2), while everywhere else on that line is 9 — so those specific cells must be where two trajectory lines cross. Now checking the r-c=2 diagonal to see if the same pattern holds.

That r-c=-6 diagonal doesn't check out as a line. Checking r+c=2, I find another valid line with values 3,9,9, and testing r-c=6 fails since (6,0) is 0. So far the valid r+c diagonals form the set {2,8,10,16}.

But testing the r-c values against the 3s and 1s breaks down—several cells don't land on the sets I found. I notice the 3/1 markers seem to form diamond shapes centered at specific coordinates, and I'm checking whether those centers align to any consistent line pattern, but nothing obvious emerges yet.

Some 3s appear where two trajectory lines intersect, like a point that sits on both an A-line and a B-line simultaneously. But not every 3 fits that intersection rule—some 3s don't correspond to any crossing point I've defined. I'm now wondering if intersections get marked 1 while the cells surrounding them get marked 3, and I want to verify this pattern against one of the diamond centers.

Testing the center at one point, its A and B values don't seem to match any of the trajectory lines, yet it's marked 1—so maybe self-intersections in the actual billiard path (cells the ball visits twice) explain the 1s rather than line intersections. I'm tracing the full bouncing path from the source, following it through each wall bounce and change of direction, to find which cells get revisited during the loop.

Checking the other direction from (5,3), going down-left instead: (6,2),(7,1),(8,0), then bouncing off the left wall to down-right (9,1), then off the bottom to up-right, which leads to (7,3) — but that cell is already occupied, so this path runs into a conflict.

I'm cross-referencing the colors along both loops to find where they overlap and whether the color values match consistently between them.

I'm noticing 1s appear only where a single loop passes, while 3s mark spots where both loops overlap. This suggests diamonds are separate objects overlaid at specific positions, with only two of their four corners landing on the loop path itself, and I'm trying to figure out where these diamond centers get placed relative to the source.

Testing whether diamonds are offset from the source by a fixed distance along the axes rather than tied to loop indices. In example 3, the offsets from source are (-4,0), (0,-4), (+4,0), with the fourth direction falling outside the grid, suggesting the rule is diamonds placed at distance 4 in each cardinal direction from the source point.

Maybe the row doesn't exist so the bottom corner is just off-grid, but the center should still print regardless. Let me try a different framing: perhaps the 3s and 1s mark where two loops cross or intersect, not just a fixed lattice offset from the source.

Looking at example 2 more carefully since it's asymmetric and useful — I'm tracing the loop from source (1,2) across all four diagonal directions to map out where it travels around the 9x9 grid.

Now I'm matching up the traced cells against the actual output colors, checking which positions got 5, 3, or 1. I'm also starting to trace a second loop heading the opposite diagonal direction, but hitting inconsistencies where a cell I expected to be part of the pattern shows 0 instead — so I need to reconsider the direction order for that loop.

Then I realize those inconsistent cells actually belong to a diamond pattern centered elsewhere, so I'm identifying the 1-valued cells in the grid as diamond centers and figuring out their offsets relative to the source point: (0,-2), (0,+2), (+2,0), (+4,0), with (-2,0) falling outside the grid. I'm checking whether the same offset pattern applies to a different example with its own source point.

Checking ex2 more carefully, I map out the 3-clusters and test whether diamond corners centered at (1,0) line up with the actual grid positions, and it seems to partially match.

Wait, (3,0) is actually 5, not 1, so the 3-lattice pattern in example 2 forms a rectangular region across even rows and odd columns, but the centers with value 1 aren't fully consistent — some expected centers like (3,0), (3,4), (5,0), (5,4) are missing.

I'm checking whether the 1s and 3s correspond to loop cells alternating by parity within that region — even rows getting 3, odd rows getting 1 — but there are exceptions like (5,2)=1 that don't fit a simple loop I've traced yet, so I need to trace which loop that cell belongs to.

Trying the up-right ray reflecting through the grid, none of the resulting coordinates match the actual 5-positions in the grid, so that path is wrong. Let me instead just list out all the 5-positions across the rows to see what pattern they actually form.

Tracing loop A, all the cells outside the region come out as 5, confirming that pattern. But (3,0) doesn't fit on loop A, so it must belong to a separate loop B that I still need to trace.

Following that other diagonal further, though, the colors don't line up with what I'd expect — some cells that should be 5 are actually 0, so the region boundary must be more complicated than a simple ray pattern. Maybe the rays terminate or decay partway through rather than continuing indefinitely, so I should go back and look at example 3 since it's cleaner and more symmetric.

Mapping out example 3's full grid, I notice diamond shapes centered around a few points, with the source diamond in the middle. But the corners of the source diamond are colored differently than in example 2 — here they match the background diamond color instead of standing out, which breaks the pattern I was assuming held across examples.

Checking distances, the three diamonds sit exactly 4 steps up, down, and left from the source, while the position 4 steps right would fall outside the grid. Now I'm cross-checking this against example 1's source at (5,3) in a 10x10 grid to see if the same offset pattern holds, but the corner and center values there don't line up cleanly, so I need to recount that row carefully.

Also checking: (1,2) itself shows full corners from shared diamonds at left and right. So ex2 has diamonds at dist2 left, dist2 right, dist2 down, and dist4 down, but not at dist2 up, dist4 left, or dist4 right since those fall off-grid or are absent. For ex1, I'm checking dist2 right, dist2 down, and dist2 up against the pattern.

But now looking at ex1 more carefully, the up direction fails and left fails too, while dist4 up and dist4 right succeed but dist4 down doesn't quite fit. This is inconsistent, so maybe the diamonds aren't placed by simple offset direction but rather trace along the spiral loop path itself. I'm mapping out loop2's index order going down-left from the source, trying to see if the diamond centers correspond to specific loop indices.

I'm now trying to trace loop1's colors from the source, going through the bounce point and each successive step, checking if a repeating pattern shows up at certain index positions.

Then I compare loop2's colors from the source similarly, and notice that the 3s and 1s seem to appear at cells shared between both loops or at specific symmetric positions, so I'm testing whether the coloring depends on cell overlap between the two loop paths rather than pure index position.

Actually, let me try a completely different angle: unfolding the grid through reflections, so the trajectory becomes a straight diagonal line through mirrored copies of the source, which might explain the 7/9/5 color pattern more cleanly.

Then I wonder if the 3/1 diamonds correspond to where reflected images of the source land back inside the actual grid, though when I check example 3's source point, folding it back doesn't cleanly line up.

I try the diamond centers against the source coordinates directly, looking at their differences relative to grid size, but reflecting across the row boundaries doesn't produce the offsets seen. Maybe instead the diamond positions come from where the diagonal rays actually cross each other rather than from wall reflections.

So diamond centers seem to occur at points where a ray returns after bouncing off two walls. Testing this on example 1 with source (5,3) on a 10x10 grid: tracing the up-right diagonal through bounces off top and right walls, it lands back at (5,5), which matches another diamond center.

I try the up-left diagonal through bounces off left and top walls, landing at (1,3) — also matching, since it shares the source's column. Similarly (5,7) comes from a down-right path bouncing off bottom then right walls, ending up in the source's row, confirming the pattern that diamond centers align with the source's row or column after two-bounce reflections.

Tracing the down-left and down-right rays from the source through their bounces, both eventually land back on the same target cells I already found — (5,3) and (9,7) — confirming the diamond markers repeat consistently regardless of which diagonal direction I trace first.

Testing the second example with source at (1,2), I trace all four diagonal rays through their bounces off each wall and find they converge on (1,0), (1,4), and (5,2), matching the same pattern of hitting a boundary and reflecting toward the center point.

I also notice the rays don't extend past their diamond center — checking the down-left path in example 2, the colors stop right at the reflection point rather than continuing further.

All the path cells match up as 5s, confirming the long diagonal path is complete. Now I'm checking whether the 3s correspond to diagonal neighbors of each diamond center, testing centers (1,0), (1,4), (5,2), (3,2), and the source itself to see if their neighboring cells account for all the 3s in the grid.

I verify this pattern holds exactly for the second example, then start rechecking against the first example using centers (1,3), (5,5), (5,7), (7,3) and their diagonal neighbors.

Tracing the diagonal ray path from (8,5), bouncing off walls until it hits row 8 or column 5, landing on center (2,5) via a series of reflections through the grid. Now I'm tracing a second ray up-right from the source, bouncing off the right wall and top wall to find the next center point.

I'm tracing two more diagonal rays going down-left and down-right from the source, bouncing off the bottom wall and side walls, finding they hit row 8 and column 11 respectively to establish centers C3 at (8,1) and C4 at (8,11).

Right, (9,10) ends up as both a path cell and a diamond corner, so it becomes a 3. I've identified all four centers and their corner cells, filtering out any that fall off-grid. Now I'm assembling the 12x12 grid, starting with zeros, marking the paths as 8s, then overlaying the corner 3s.

I'm tracing out each path's full list of coordinates, plus the source cell at (8,5) marked as 8. Now I'm working row by row, noting where 8s and 3s land, including the overlap case where a path cell at (1,4) gets overridden by its corner value of 3.

Continuing to fill in rows 7-11 values, noting where paths overlap with corners get colored 3 (e.g. (9,0),(9,10)), consistent with the pattern seen in example 1 where corner-path overlaps were colored 3.
